title: The Akathist
hook: a Byzantine hymn to Mary sung standing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the oldest Marian prayer, the Sub tuum praesidium: people running for cover together. Your line was we fly to thee. Did you say we instead of I? Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

Here is a hymn whose name is an instruction about chairs. In the Byzantine churches, the Orthodox and the Eastern Catholic churches, there's a long hymn to Mary that nobody sits down for. Its name, the Akathist, means not sitting. The church fills, the singing starts, and the people stay on their feet, stanza after stanza, while one greeting comes around again and again: rejoice. A story people tell says it was once sung through a whole night, standing, by a city giving thanks for being saved from a siege. Whatever its history, the posture stuck. Today's word is the hymn sung standing.
screen: `A HYMN NAMED FOR NOT SITTING.` → `THE PEOPLE STAY ON THEIR FEET.` → `REJOICE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Akathistos, in Greek, means not seated. Standing is what a person does when someone they honor walks into the room. The hymn makes that a whole service: the body says what the words are saying. Some people stand to show respect; some stand because they can't sit still with joy. This hymn asks for both. Next, the greeting. The word that keeps returning is chaire, rejoice, or hail. It's the angel's word. In Luke's Gospel, Gabriel opens with it, which the Douay-Rheims renders "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." The Akathist takes that one greeting and multiplies it, line after line, each rejoice hung with a new picture of Mary, the way the Litany of Loreto stacks its names. And at the end of each long stanza comes the refrain: rejoice, unwedded bride. Third, the story underneath. The hymn doesn't only praise; it walks through the Gospel. Gabriel's visit. The birth. The shepherds. The magi following the star. The rejoices come out of the story, like applause that rises at each turn of a play. Fourth, where it lives. Eastern churches sing it especially in Lent, and that includes the Byzantine Catholic churches, in full communion with Rome. For a Latin Catholic, it's a reminder that the Church breathes, in a phrase Pope John Paul the Second used, with two lungs, East and West. The same Mary, the same angel's word, said in a different key, and on your feet.
screen: `AKATHISTOS: NOT SEATED.` · `CHAIRE: THE ANGEL'S WORD.` · `THE GOSPEL STORY UNDERNEATH.` · `EAST AND WEST, TWO LUNGS.` · then, large: `REJOICE, UNWEDDED BRIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand while you pray. If you're able, stand up now. If you can't, sit up tall, and let that be your standing. Feet steady. Shoulders loose. Notice whether it feels any different from slumping, the way you'd straighten if someone had just walked in. Breathe. If you pray, you can say the angel's greeting, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, or the Akathist's refrain, rejoice, unwedded bride, once with each slow breath. If you don't, simply stand in honor of someone you love, and let your body say it. The bell holds the time.
The Akathist. A Byzantine hymn to Mary, its name meaning not seated: a chain of rejoices, built on the angel's greeting and the Gospel story, sung on your feet. Today's word.
Your line: sung standing. Today, stand up for one thing you'd normally do sitting, a call, a prayer, a greeting, and let your body pay attention. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians sing the Akathist to the Mother of God standing, especially in Lent, and some pray it at home or in shorter parts through the week.

notes: The meaning of the name (akathistos, 'not seated') is stated; it is the standard sense of the Greek and the source of the index carry 'sung standing'. Confirm under the claims rule.
The siege story (traditionally the deliverance of Constantinople) is told only as 'a story people tell', without naming the city, date or enemy.
Claim that the hymn's first part walks through the Gospel story (Annunciation, Nativity, shepherds, magi); confirm.
Refrain rendered 'rejoice, unwedded bride' (Greek Χαῖρε, Νύμφη ἀνύμφευτε); the English is the script's own. Confirm.
'Especially in Lent' (the Saturday of the Akathist and Lenten Fridays in Byzantine use); stated without counts. Confirm.
'Two lungs' image is attributed to John Paul II (Ut Unum Sint 54; also elsewhere); paraphrased. Confirm reference.
Practice repeats the angel's greeting as a prayer line; no new prayer written.
